skill.name: openclaw-secure-linux-cloud
skill.description: Secure OpenClaw self-hosting guidance for Linux cloud servers, with private access, Podman deployment, token authentication, sandboxing, and exposure review.
skill.summary: Guides private-first OpenClaw deployment and hardening on Linux cloud hosts.
skill.author: xixu-me

security_audit.summary: The skill is legitimate security guidance, and many SKILL.md alerts are Markdown false positives. However, the reference includes privileged host changes, persistent service enablement, token display, and root execution of project scripts from a cloned repository. These commands require strong user confirmation and safer installation guidance before publication.

remediation.issue: Root execution of project setup scripts from cloned source
remediation.suggestion: Use pinned releases, checksum or signature verification, script review steps, and rootless setup paths where possible.

remediation.issue: Copy-paste privileged changes to SSH and firewall configuration
remediation.suggestion: Add explicit preflight checks, backups, rollback steps, and warnings before reload or firewall activation.

remediation.issue: Gateway token is displayed from a hidden environment file
remediation.suggestion: Avoid printing full tokens. Provide verification and rotation guidance that masks secret values.

remediation.issue: Debian and Ubuntu commands may be reused on unsupported hosts
remediation.suggestion: Gate command output on distro detection and provide non-Debian branches only after validation.

content.value_statement: Self-hosting OpenClaw on a cloud server can expose a powerful control plane. This skill guides private deployment with SSH tunneling, Podman, token auth, sandboxing, and firewall checks.
actual_capabilities: Explains a private-first OpenClaw architecture for Linux cloud hosts.
Compares SSH tunnels, Tailscale, and reverse proxies for remote access.
Provides Debian and Ubuntu example commands for host hardening and Podman setup.
Defines conservative defaults for token auth, pairing, tools, and sandboxing.
Lists pre-launch and day-two audit checks for services and permissions.
limitations: Commands are Debian and Ubuntu oriented and may need distro changes.
It does not verify current upstream OpenClaw commands automatically.
Users must review privileged commands before running them.
It is not a full Linux hardening baseline for unrelated systems.

use_cases.title: Plan a private deployment
use_cases.description: Create a secure first-run plan for OpenClaw on a new Linux VPS.

use_cases.title: Review an exposed host
use_cases.description: Identify risky OpenClaw exposure and prioritize safer access controls.

use_cases.title: Choose an access model
use_cases.description: Compare SSH tunneling, Tailscale, and reverse proxy options for remote control.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a first deployment
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me deploy OpenClaw on a Linux VPS with private access only. Ask for blocking details first.

prompt_templates.title: Check my current setup
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my OpenClaw cloud setup for exposure risks. Focus on network binding, auth, sandboxing, and permissions.

prompt_templates.title: Compare access options
prompt_templates.prompt: Compare SSH tunnel, Tailscale, and reverse proxy access for my OpenClaw host. Recommend the lowest-risk path.

prompt_templates.title: Build a hardening runbook
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a staged OpenClaw hardening runbook with validation steps, rollback notes, and commands separated by local and server context.

output_examples.input: I want OpenClaw on a VPS for personal use only.
output: Recommended path: keep the gateway private and use an SSH tunnel.
Harden SSH and firewall rules before OpenClaw becomes reachable.
Use narrow tool permissions and keep sandboxing enabled.

output_examples.input: My OpenClaw UI is reachable from the internet.
output: Immediate concern: public Control UI exposure increases risk even with token auth.
Move access behind a private path first, then review auth and logs.
Consider a reverse proxy only when public access is required.

output_examples.input: Should I use Tailscale or a reverse proxy?
output: Use Tailscale when trusted devices need repeated private access.
Use a reverse proxy only for a clear public access requirement.
Keep loopback binding as the baseline unless the design changes deliberately.

best_practices: Confirm the target host and distro before using package or firewall commands.
Keep OpenClaw private by default and expose it only after a documented need.
Review privileged commands with the user before execution.
anti_patterns: Binding the gateway to all interfaces during first setup.
Treating token authentication as a replacement for network boundaries.
Running broad tool permissions before the workflow requires them.

faq.question: Does this skill install OpenClaw automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides guidance and example commands that users must review before use.

faq.question: Which platforms does it target?
faq.answer: It targets Linux cloud hosts, with Debian and Ubuntu examples in the reference.

faq.question: Why does it prefer SSH tunneling?
faq.answer: SSH tunneling keeps the Control UI private while the user validates the deployment.

faq.question: Can it help with Tailscale?
faq.answer: Yes. It explains when Tailscale is useful for repeated private access across trusted devices.

faq.question: Does it support public reverse proxy deployment?
faq.answer: It discusses reverse proxy use only when public access is required and extra safeguards are accepted.

faq.question: Why are privileged commands included?
faq.answer: Host hardening often needs elevated commands. Users should inspect each command before running it.
